fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, tells Timothy, his true child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2), to "…appeal to him as to a father." I think that's a gentler way to say a hard thing. Same message, softer landing.

Paul doesn't mention savings at all. He describes her as truly in need and left all alone. A cookie jar of coins isn't the picture. She "…puts her hope in God…" and continues night and day in her petitions and prayers.
Yes! Paul says, "Treat younger men as brothers…" After the father for the older man, the family picture keeps going. Brothers is the word he picks for the younger men.
Aunts don't make Paul's list. He names fathers, mothers, brothers and sisters. For the older women, the word is "…mothers…" Same family picture, just a different word.

Paul doesn't say that anywhere in this passage. Past sins don't come up in these verses at all. What he says is that repaying parents "…is pleasing in the sight of God." Picture a grown kid who keeps showing up for Mom, week after week, with no trophy and no applause. Paul says God is pleased by that kind of repaying.

Yes, baker. The widow who is truly in need and left all alone "…puts her hope in God…" And Paul says she continues night and day in her petitions and prayers. Her hope sits with God, and her days are full of prayer.

Paul doesn't say neighbors. He says she is left all alone and "…puts her hope in God…" I think being left alone makes that line stand out even more. She continues night and day in her petitions and prayers.

That's what Paul says: "…she who lives for pleasure is dead even while she is still alive." That's a strong picture, and he puts it right next to the widow who prays night and day. One lives for pleasure and the other puts her hope in God.

Close, but Paul sets the bar higher. He says a widow should be enrolled if she is "…at least sixty years old…" Fifty is a fine number, but it's ten years short of what Paul writes. Sorry, fifty, you almost made the list.

Paul says something very different. He says they "…will also learn to be idle, going from house to house…" Then he adds that they'd be not only idle, but gossips and busybodies too. Devoting herself to every good work is how he describes the enrolled widow back in verse 10.

True. Paul says, "For some have already turned aside to follow Satan." That's a heavy line, and we can let it be heavy. It comes right after he advises the younger widows to marry, have children and manage their households.

Paul does say it, baker: "For some have already turned aside to follow Satan." It's a heavy verse. He says it right after telling the younger widows to marry, have children and manage their households. So the statement is true.
